name: Money Talks
subject: Money, markets and economics
tagline: Twenty questions on cash, crashes, coins and the people who move markets. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: Which New York street is shorthand for the whole of American high finance?
questions.w: Wall Street, home of the New York Stock Exchange since traders signed an agreement under a buttonwood tree there in 1792.
questions.more: The street is named after a wooden wall the Dutch built in 1653 to keep the English and the Lenape out of New Amsterdam. Most big banks have long since moved to Midtown, but the name stuck. Madison Avenue plays the same role for advertising.

questions.q: In the abbreviation ATM, the cash machine, what does the M stand for?
questions.w: Machine: automated teller machine. A teller is the bank clerk it replaced.
questions.more: The first one was installed at a Barclays branch in north London in June 1967 and opened by the sitcom actor Reg Varney; it used paper vouchers soaked in a mildly radioactive ink. The four-digit PIN exists because its inventor's wife said she could not remember six. There are now more than three million machines worldwide, and the number is falling.

questions.q: What does the stock-market phrase 'bull market' mean?
questions.w: Prices are rising, as opposed to a bear market, when they fall by a fifth or more.
questions.more: The usual explanation is the way the animals attack: a bull thrusts its horns up, a bear swipes its paws down. The bronze Charging Bull near Wall Street was dumped there without permission one night in 1989 by the sculptor Arturo Di Modica, as a gift after the 1987 crash. The city let it stay.

questions.q: Which card company's adverts told you that for everything else, there's this?
questions.w: Mastercard, whose 'Priceless' campaign began in 1997 and ran in more than a hundred countries.
questions.more: Mastercard began in 1966 as Interbank, a group of banks fighting back against Bank of America's BankAmericard, which became Visa. The two companies do not lend any money themselves; they run the networks and take a small slice of every swipe, which made them two of the most valuable companies on earth.

questions.q: The euro notes and coins went into people's pockets in twelve countries on 1 January of which year?
questions.w: 2002. The euro had existed on paper since 1999, but the cash arrived three years later.
questions.more: It was the biggest currency changeover in history, with 15 billion notes and 50 billion coins. The notes show imaginary bridges and windows, so no country could claim one, though a Dutch town later built all seven bridges for real. Twenty countries use it today; Britain, Sweden and Denmark chose to keep their own.

questions.q: The Wall Street Crash that set off the Great Depression happened in which year?
questions.w: 1929. Black Thursday on 24 October was followed by Black Monday and Black Tuesday the next week.
questions.more: The market had nearly quintupled in the 1920s on borrowed money. By 1932 it had lost 89 per cent of its value and did not regain its 1929 peak until 1954. The widely repeated image of ruined brokers leaping from windows is largely myth; suicides in New York actually fell that autumn.

questions.q: Which flower set off what is often called the first speculative bubble, in the Netherlands in the 1630s?
questions.w: The tulip. At the peak in early 1637, single bulbs of rare striped varieties changed hands for the price of a canal house.
questions.more: The prized flame patterns were caused by a virus that also weakened the bulbs. Much of the trading was in futures, promises to buy bulbs still in the ground, over tavern tables. Modern historians think the mania was smaller and the crash less ruinous than the famous Victorian accounts claimed.

questions.q: What does a central bank usually do to fight inflation?
questions.w: Raise interest rates, making borrowing dearer and saving more attractive, so people and businesses spend less.
questions.more: Paul Volcker's Federal Reserve pushed US rates to 20 per cent in 1981 to break inflation, at the cost of a deep recession and angry farmers blockading its headquarters with tractors. Taxes are set by governments, not central banks. The Fed's rate decisions move markets around the world within seconds.

questions.q: Which Scottish economist's 1776 book The Wealth of Nations described an 'invisible hand' guiding self-interested traders to serve the public good?
questions.w: Adam Smith, a professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow who was once kidnapped by travellers as a child.
questions.more: The famous phrase appears only once in the 950-page book. Smith also argued for public schools and warned against merchants conspiring to raise prices, which disappoints some of his modern fans. He appeared on the Bank of England twenty-pound note from 2007 to 2020, the first Scot on an English note.

questions.q: In 2008 which Wall Street bank's collapse, the largest bankruptcy in American history, turned the credit crunch into a global financial crisis?
questions.w: Lehman Brothers, 158 years old, which filed on 15 September 2008 with 619 billion dollars of debt.
questions.more: Bear Stearns had been rescued and sold to JPMorgan in March, and Merrill Lynch was sold to Bank of America the same weekend Lehman fell. Regulators let Lehman go to avoid rewarding recklessness and then spent trillions propping up everyone else. Employees were photographed leaving with their belongings in cardboard boxes; the image defined the crisis.

questions.q: In which country did the worst hyperinflation ever recorded take place, with prices doubling every 15 hours in 1946?
questions.w: Hungary, which printed a 100 quintillion pengő note, the highest denomination ever issued.
questions.more: Weimar Germany's 1923 inflation, with wheelbarrows of marks, is more famous but milder: prices doubled every few days. Zimbabwe's 2008 episode produced a hundred-trillion-dollar note now sold to tourists. Hungary replaced the pengő with the forint in August 1946, at a rate of 400 octillion to one.
